title: Priority 3: Changing How Funding Flows
author: Michael B. Horn, Danny Curtis, Angela Jackson and Mallory Dwinal-Palisch
summary: This is the fourth of six Clayton Christensen Institute papers offering a state policy playbook for integrated education-to-career systems, republished on Michael Horn's Substack. It argues that institutions follow the money, so states must redesign funding if they want schools, colleges and training providers to launch and sustain career-connected pathways. The paper makes three recommendations, each tied to a state example and to business model theory. States should seed new programs with startup grants, as in the California Apprenticeship Initiative. They should shift a meaningful share of funding from inputs to outcomes, as Texas did with its returned-value formula for Texas State Technical College. They should also create portable learner-centered accounts, as Indiana did with Career Scholarship Accounts. Each section includes a Chesterton's Fence caution and concrete takeaways for other states.
points: Institutions organize around what legacy funding rewards, so career-connected learning needs new cost structures rather than only new programs.
Startup grants act like early-stage capital that lets incumbents run a new model alongside the old one, but they should target demonstrated demand and a credible plan for sustaining the pathway.
Texas tied all of TSTC's instruction and administration funding to post-exit wages, and a clear, undiluted formula was credited with changing institutional behavior.
Indiana's Career Scholarship Accounts give students up to 5,000 dollars a year across approved providers, with demand outstripping the funding cap and transparency still lacking.
Each recommendation carries a Chesterton's Fence caution about unintended effects, such as narrowed access or metrics that distort institutional missions.
quotes: It should come as no surprise that learning providers organize themselves around enrollment, seat-time, and traditional classroom learning because those are the activities legacy state money rewards and supports; institutional behavior almost always follows where the funding flows.

Without funding models that support these costs, even promising programs will remain dependent on short-term grants, heroic staff effort, or informal workarounds. That instability makes it difficult to sustain and scale successful programs.

A limited-term startup grant does not fundamentally change an institution’s financial formula—more durable funding reforms are still needed. But it can provide the free cash flow necessary to launch a new model in parallel with the existing one.
Just as important, outcomes-based funding doesn’t specify operational moves. It changes the financial logic and lets institutions innovate within that new set of incentives.

Texas tied 100 percent of TSTC’s state funding for instruction and administration to the labor-market outcomes the college produced. TSTC leaders themselves opposed proposals to water down the formula by splitting its funds between enrollment and earnings.

When students choose among approved opportunities, providers compete for their participation and revenue. This can encourage employers, training providers, colleges, and other support organizations to reorganize their resources, processes, and financial formulas to better serve high school students.
From the first to the second year of the program, funding doubled from $5 million to $10 million, while participation increased more than eightfold, from 234 students to roughly 1,900.
